pathway.title: Software Development
pathway.description: Learn a disciplined path from software needs and requirements through design, implementation, verification, release, and maintenance.

course.title: Software Development — Advanced
course.short_description: An advanced software-development course in system design, distributed consistency, workload and data scaling, resilience, security, SLOs, incident response, disaster recovery, and progressive delivery.
course.prerequisites: Completion of Software Development — Intermediate or equivalent experience with domain modelling, APIs, persistence, automated testing, security basics, CI, observability, and release planning.
learning_outcomes: Translate quality attributes and workload assumptions into capacity budgets and architecture trade-offs.
Design service boundaries, consistency rules, and repeat-safe distributed workflows.
Plan compatible data evolution, bounded workloads, and dependency failure containment.
Apply threat modelling, least privilege, SLI/SLO policy, and incident coordination.
Specify tested recovery objectives and progressive release controls with explicit operational evidence.
course.dependencies: Python 3.10+ standard library only; no third-party packages required.

modules.title: Architect distributed systems deliberately
modules.description: Translate quality attributes into capacity budgets, choose capability boundaries, and design consistency for distributed workflows.

topics.title: Turn quality attributes into capacity budgets
topics.description: Translate reliability, latency, throughput, and growth needs into measurable architecture constraints.

lesson.title: Turn quality attributes into capacity budgets
objectives: Convert stakeholder quality goals into measurable service targets.
Estimate peak workload and identify the dominant capacity constraint.
State assumptions and uncertainty instead of treating estimates as guarantees.

blocks.title: System-design principle
blocks.body: System design starts with workload and quality goals, not a diagram of fashionable components. Translate a statement such as “the service should feel fast” into a latency objective, identify the percentile and user journey, then estimate normal and peak request rates. For example, a fictional county produce cooperative might see morning order bursts rather than a uniform daily average. Separate reads, writes, background jobs, payload size, and expensive operations; each creates different pressure. A simple budget can multiply requests per second by average work per request, but capacity also depends on storage, network, concurrency, and dependency limits. Add headroom for bursts and failure modes, then state which measurement would replace each assumption. Estimates help compare options; they do not predict production perfectly. Revisit them with representative load tests and observed telemetry, and design graceful degradation before scaling a guessed bottleneck.

blocks.title: Run the small model
blocks.code:
peak_orders_per_second = 180
reads_per_order = 4
read_capacity = peak_orders_per_second * reads_per_order
headroom = 1.5
print(read_capacity, int(read_capacity * headroom))
blocks.explanation: This small, executable model isolates one decision about turn quality attributes into capacity budgets. It is a reasoning aid, not a performance benchmark or deployment guarantee. Change its inputs, identify the assumptions it omits, then compare its behavior with the stated system constraint.

blocks.title: Design flow
blocks.alt_text: A user journey is translated into workload estimates and service objectives, then tested to identify a measured bottleneck.
blocks.content: user journey → workload model → latency/reliability objective → capacity budget → measured bottleneck

blocks.title: Design exercise
instructions: For a fictional produce-order service, estimate a peak of 180 order requests per second, four catalogue reads per order, and 50 percent headroom. List assumptions, the first capacity limit to measure, and one safe degradation behavior.
success_checks: The artifact names assumptions, boundaries, and a measurable decision.
A test, calculation, or inspection step can challenge the decision.
Failure behavior, limitations, and an owner or revisit trigger are recorded.

revision_notes: Begin with workload and user-visible objectives.

topics.title: Choose service boundaries and ownership deliberately
topics.description: Use domain cohesion, change patterns, and operational ownership to choose modular and distributed boundaries.

lesson.title: Choose service boundaries and ownership deliberately
objectives: Compare a modular monolith and independently deployed services.
Assign data and operational ownership to clear boundaries.
Recognize when network distribution creates more cost than value.

blocks.title: System-design principle
blocks.body: A service boundary should reflect cohesive business responsibility, a stable contract, and a team or operational owner—not merely a folder or database table. A modular monolith can enforce boundaries while keeping local calls and simpler transactions; it is often an effective starting point when a team is small or workload is not independently constrained. A separately deployed service can scale, fail, and release independently, but adds network latency, partial failure, security policy, deployment coordination, and data consistency work. Avoid sharing writable tables across proposed service boundaries: it hides ownership and couples releases. For a fictional regional logistics platform, inventory reservation and delivery dispatch might eventually have different scaling and ownership needs, but that is a hypothesis to validate from change frequency and load. Draw the boundary, state which capability owns each datum, define its API and failure contract, and name the evidence that would justify splitting or merging it later.

blocks.title: Run the small model
blocks.explanation: This small, executable model isolates one decision about choose service boundaries and ownership deliberately. blocks.title: Design flow

topics.title: Design consistency and idempotent distributed workflows
topics.description: Reason about retries, duplicate delivery, consistency, and multi-step business operations.

lesson.title: Design consistency and idempotent distributed workflows
objectives: Distinguish atomic local transactions from distributed workflows.
Design idempotency keys and duplicate handling for retries.
Explain saga and outbox patterns with their limits.

blocks.title: System-design principle
blocks.body: A timeout does not tell a caller whether a remote operation failed before it committed or succeeded before its response was lost. Retrying a non-idempotent operation can create duplicate orders or charges. Give a command a stable idempotency key, persist the key with the outcome, and return the same result for a repeated request within a documented scope and retention period. A database transaction can protect changes within one database, but it cannot atomically include an unrelated broker or external service. An outbox stores the domain change and an event record in the same local transaction; a publisher later delivers the event, while consumers deduplicate. A saga coordinates steps with compensating actions, but compensation is not always a true reversal and may itself fail. State which consistency is required for each view, where delay is acceptable, how operators detect stuck work, and how reconciliation resolves uncertainty. Never claim exactly-once effects merely because a queue retries messages.

blocks.title: Run the small model
blocks.code:
seen = {"order-42": {"status": "reserved", "result": 1}}
key = "order-42"
result = seen.setdefault(key, {"status": "reserved", "result": 2})
print(result["result"], len(seen))
blocks.explanation: This small, executable model isolates one decision about design consistency and idempotent distributed workflows. It is a reasoning aid, not a performance benchmark or deployment guarantee. Change its inputs, identify the assumptions it omits, then compare its behavior with the stated system constraint.

blocks.title: Design flow
blocks.alt_text: A command uses an idempotency key, commits state and outbox together, then tolerates repeated event delivery through consumer deduplication.
blocks.content: command + idempotency key → local transaction (state + outbox) → at-least-once delivery → deduplicating consumer

blocks.title: Design exercise
instructions: Design a fictional order-reservation request that may time out after committing. Specify key scope, stored response, expiry, outbox event, duplicate consumer behavior, and manual reconciliation path.

items.prompt: What does an outbox pattern atomically persist?

choices.text: A guarantee of exactly-once delivery

revision_notes: A timeout may leave a write outcome unknown.

modules.title: Design reliable data and workload paths
modules.description: Scale data safely, bound work, apply backpressure, and contain dependency failures.

topics.title: Scale data with partitioning and compatible migrations
topics.description: Design indexes and partitions from access patterns, and evolve schemas safely across releases.

lesson.title: Scale data with partitioning and compatible migrations
objectives: Choose indexes from measured query patterns and write costs.
Explain partitioning and its operational trade-offs.
Plan expand-migrate-contract schema changes for rolling releases.

blocks.title: System-design principle
blocks.body: Data scaling begins with access patterns: which records are fetched together, how queries filter and sort, how hot a key becomes, and how write frequency competes with reads. An index can reduce lookup work but increases storage and write amplification; measure its effect rather than adding indexes by intuition. Partitioning can distribute large datasets or isolate retention windows, but introduces routing, rebalancing, cross-partition queries, and hot-partition risk. Schema changes must coexist with old and new application versions during a rolling deployment. An expand-migrate-contract sequence first adds a backward-compatible field or table, deploys code that can read both and write safely, backfills in bounded batches, verifies data, then removes the old representation in a later release. Define resumability, progress visibility, rate limits, and abort behavior. Backups are not a substitute for a tested migration recovery plan, and destructive transformations need verified restore points and explicit ownership.

blocks.title: Run the small model
blocks.code:
queries_per_minute = 12000
index_hit_rate = 0.92
indexed = int(queries_per_minute * index_hit_rate)
print(indexed, queries_per_minute - indexed)
blocks.explanation: This small, executable model isolates one decision about scale data with partitioning and compatible migrations. It is a reasoning aid, not a performance benchmark or deployment guarantee. Change its inputs, identify the assumptions it omits, then compare its behavior with the stated system constraint.

blocks.title: Design flow
blocks.alt_text: A safe schema change expands compatibility, migrates data in bounded batches, verifies it, and contracts only in a later release.
blocks.content: expand schema → dual-compatible application → bounded backfill → verify → contract in a later release

blocks.title: Design exercise
instructions: Plan a nullable `delivery_window` field for a rolling release. Specify expand, compatible code, backfill batches, verification query, rollback limit, and when the old field can be removed.
success_checks: The artifact names assumptions, boundaries, and a measurable decision.
A test, calculation, or inspection step can challenge the decision.

topics.title: Control load with caching, queues, and backpressure
topics.description: Protect constrained dependencies by bounding work, managing cache behavior, and applying admission control.

lesson.title: Control load with caching, queues, and backpressure
objectives: Identify stale-read and cache-invalidation risks.
Use bounded queues and backpressure to prevent overload amplification.
Choose admission and degradation policies that protect core operations.

blocks.title: System-design principle
blocks.body: Caching can reduce repeated reads, but it creates a second representation whose freshness and invalidation rules must be understood. Define whether stale data is acceptable, for how long, and how a cache miss behaves during a dependency outage. A cache stampede occurs when many callers recompute the same expired entry; request coalescing, jittered expiry, and bounded concurrency can reduce the burst. Queues smooth short-term work only when producers cannot grow them without limit. If arrival rate exceeds service rate, queue depth and delay increase until memory, storage, or user patience is exhausted. Backpressure communicates that capacity is constrained: reject, defer, shed optional work, or slow producers using explicit policy. Prioritize correctness-critical reservations over optional recommendations, and make fairness visible. Monitor queue age as well as depth, because a small queue containing old work can still violate a service objective. Test full queues and cold caches, not only the healthy steady state.

blocks.title: Run the small model
blocks.code:
from collections import deque
capacity = 3
queue = deque()
accepted = 0
for task in range(5):
    if len(queue) < capacity:
        queue.append(task); accepted += 1
print(accepted, len(queue))
blocks.explanation: This small, executable model isolates one decision about control load with caching, queues, and backpressure. It is a reasoning aid, not a performance benchmark or deployment guarantee. Change its inputs, identify the assumptions it omits, then compare its behavior with the stated system constraint.

blocks.title: Design flow
blocks.alt_text: Producers pass bounded admission into a monitored queue and worker pool that protect a constrained dependency.
blocks.content: producer → bounded admission → queue with age/size signals → worker pool → protected dependency

blocks.title: Design exercise
instructions: For a fictional order service with a slower stock database, define a queue limit, maximum queue age, overload response, priority rule, cache freshness rule, and operator signal.
success_checks: The artifact names assumptions, boundaries, and a measurable decision.
A test, calculation, or inspection step can challenge the decision.
Failure behavior, limitations, and an owner or revisit trigger are recorded.

items.prompt: Why must a work queue be bounded?

choices.text: To ensure every task is processed immediately

items.prompt: Why monitor queue age as well as depth?

choices.text: Age measures database storage

revision_notes: Caches trade freshness complexity for reduced repeated work.

topics.title: Contain failures with timeouts, retries, and bulkheads
topics.description: Prevent dependency failures from cascading by setting deadlines, bounded retries, and isolation boundaries.

lesson.title: Contain failures with timeouts, retries, and bulkheads
objectives: Allocate an end-to-end deadline across dependency calls.
Use bounded retries with exponential backoff and jitter for safe operations.
Explain circuit breakers, bulkheads, and failure-mode testing.

blocks.title: System-design principle
blocks.body: A slow dependency can consume every worker or connection in its caller, turning one local delay into a system-wide outage. Set a request deadline and allocate smaller timeouts to each downstream call so the overall budget remains meaningful. Retry only failures likely to be transient and only when the operation is safe to repeat; cap attempts, use exponential backoff with jitter, and avoid synchronized retry storms. A circuit breaker temporarily stops calls to a failing dependency, but needs thresholds, a recovery probe, and fallback behavior appropriate to the business operation. Bulkheads isolate pools or concurrency so one dependency cannot exhaust all capacity. Fail fast for an optional recommendation but do not silently invent a successful stock reservation. Track timeout rate, retry count, breaker state, and user-facing outcome. Exercise dependency slowness, partial responses, and recovery in tests; a happy-path simulation does not prove resilience under real infrastructure behavior.

blocks.title: Run the small model
blocks.code:
delays = [1, 2, 4]
base_ms = 250
waits = [base_ms * factor for factor in delays]
print(waits, sum(waits))
blocks.explanation: This small, executable model isolates one decision about contain failures with timeouts, retries, and bulkheads. It is a reasoning aid, not a performance benchmark or deployment guarantee. Change its inputs, identify the assumptions it omits, then compare its behavior with the stated system constraint.

blocks.title: Design flow
blocks.alt_text: A request deadline bounds dependency calls and retries, with breakers and bulkheads containing failure before an explicit fallback.
blocks.content: request deadline → bounded call timeout → limited jittered retry → breaker/bulkhead → explicit fallback

blocks.title: Design exercise
instructions: Design failure policy for stock lookup, payment confirmation, and optional product recommendations. For each, set timeout, retry safety, attempt cap, isolation, and user-visible fallback.
success_checks: The artifact names assumptions, boundaries, and a measurable decision.
A test, calculation, or inspection step can challenge the decision.
Failure behavior, limitations, and an owner or revisit trigger are recorded.

items.prompt: When is retrying a write safe?

choices.text: Whenever the client receives a timeout
When the error message is long

items.prompt: What is a bulkhead intended to do?

choices.text: Guarantee consistent distributed transactions

revision_notes: Deadlines and bounded retries limit failure amplification.

Bulkheads isolate capacity; fallbacks must preserve truthful business outcomes.

modules.title: Secure and operate production systems
modules.description: Threat-model identity boundaries, define SLOs, and coordinate incident learning.

topics.title: Threat-model distributed systems and identity boundaries
topics.description: Map trust boundaries, service identities, data sensitivity, and supply-chain risks before choosing controls.

lesson.title: Threat-model distributed systems and identity boundaries
objectives: Map assets, actors, trust zones, and abuse cases.
Apply least privilege to users, services, and deployment identities.
Prioritize mitigations and record residual security risk.

blocks.title: System-design principle
blocks.body: A distributed system creates multiple trust boundaries: browser to API, service to service, worker to queue, and deployment pipeline to production. Start by identifying valuable assets such as credentials, personal data, order state, and signing keys, then list actors, entry points, and plausible misuse. A service identity should receive only the permissions required for its role, with rotation and revocation ownership defined. Validate authorization at each boundary rather than trusting a network location or client-supplied identifier. Protect secrets in storage and logs, constrain outbound access where practical, and keep dependency and build provenance reviewable. A threat model is not complete when a checklist is filled; rank impact and likelihood, select a control, decide how it will be tested, and record residual risk. Use fictional data in learning examples. Security controls may introduce latency or operational work, so document the trade-off and revisit it when an integration, data class, or deployment trust boundary changes.

topics.title: Design observability with SLIs, SLOs, and error budgets
topics.description: Turn user-visible reliability into measured indicators and operational decision rules.

lesson.title: Design observability with SLIs, SLOs, and error budgets
objectives: Define an SLI from a user-visible event and a measurement window.
Set an SLO that reflects service expectations and failure cost.
Use error budgets as a decision aid rather than a guarantee.

blocks.title: System-design principle
blocks.body: An indicator (SLI) is a measured proportion or distribution tied to a user-visible service outcome, such as successful order confirmations within a latency target. An objective (SLO) states the desired level over a defined window; it should exclude neither inconvenient failures nor important parts of the journey without explanation. If 99.5 percent of 20,000 eligible operations must succeed, the arithmetic gives an error budget of 100 failures in that window. The number is a policy input, not permission to fail exactly 100 times or proof that failures are evenly distributed. Segmenting by operation and customer impact can reveal localized harm that a global number hides. Define event eligibility, data source, alert threshold, and owner before using an SLO to guide release speed. Pair metrics with traces and structured logs for diagnosis, redact sensitive values, and alert on actionable symptoms rather than every internal fluctuation.

blocks.title: Run the small model
blocks.code:
eligible = 20000
slo = 0.995
budget = int(eligible * (1 - slo))
print(budget)
blocks.explanation: This small, executable model isolates one decision about design observability with slis, slos, and error budgets. It is a reasoning aid, not a performance benchmark or deployment guarantee. Change its inputs, identify the assumptions it omits, then compare its behavior with the stated system constraint.

blocks.alt_text: User-visible events feed a measured indicator and objective, whose error budget informs operational and release decisions.

topics.title: Lead incident response and blameless learning
topics.description: Coordinate incident roles, safe mitigation, communication, evidence preservation, and corrective action.

lesson.title: Lead incident response and blameless learning
objectives: Separate incident coordination from technical investigation.
Choose reversible mitigations that reduce user harm.
Write follow-up actions that improve system conditions rather than assign blame.

blocks.title: System-design principle
blocks.body: An incident is a time-sensitive coordination problem as well as a technical fault. Establish severity from user impact and data risk, appoint an incident lead, keep a shared timeline, and assign communication and investigation roles when the event warrants them. First stabilize the service with the least risky reversible mitigation: disable an optional feature, shed nonessential load, or roll back a known-bad change. Avoid destructive repairs before preserving relevant evidence and confirming data integrity. Communicate what is known, what is uncertain, and when the next update will arrive; do not speculate or expose personal information. After recovery, review contributing conditions such as unsafe defaults, inadequate capacity, confusing alerts, or an untested migration. A blameless review is not an absence of accountability; it shifts attention from individual fault to the system conditions that made an error possible and hard to detect. Assign corrective work with an owner, observable completion criteria, and a follow-up date.

modules.title: Recover, release, and evolve systems
modules.description: Practice disaster recovery, progressive delivery, and evidence-led architecture synthesis.

topics.title: Engineer backup, restore, and disaster recovery objectives
topics.description: Define recovery point and time objectives, test restoration, and account for dependencies and regional failure.

lesson.title: Engineer backup, restore, and disaster recovery objectives
objectives: Distinguish RPO from RTO and connect both to business impact.
Design backup retention and access controls for recovery scenarios.
Plan and test a restore, failover, and post-recovery verification.

blocks.title: System-design principle
blocks.body: A backup is useful only if it can be restored into a trustworthy service state. Recovery Point Objective (RPO) describes the maximum tolerable data-loss window; Recovery Time Objective (RTO) describes the target time to restore an agreed service. They arise from business impact, not from a storage product's defaults. Define what is backed up—database, object media, configuration, encryption keys, and infrastructure definitions—and protect copies from the same account or region failure that could affect production. Retention, immutability, access separation, and restore credentials matter as much as schedule. A recovery runbook should specify dependencies, ordering, integrity checks, DNS or traffic switching, communication, and the choice between failback and continuing in a recovery environment. Practice restores in an isolated environment using synthetic data, record measured duration and data gap, and update objectives if evidence misses the target. Never call a snapshot a verified backup until restoration has been exercised.

blocks.title: Run the small model
blocks.code:
rpo_minutes = 15
rto_minutes = 90
restore_test_minutes = 72
print(restore_test_minutes <= rto_minutes, rpo_minutes)

topics.title: Release safely with canaries, feature controls, and rollback plans
topics.description: Limit release exposure, observe guardrails, and choose rollback or forward recovery deliberately.

lesson.title: Release safely with canaries, feature controls, and rollback plans
objectives: Define canary cohorts and user-impact guardrails.
Use feature controls safely with ownership and expiry.
Distinguish code rollback from data recovery or forward fix.

blocks.title: System-design principle
blocks.body: Progressive delivery lowers the number of users exposed to a change before evidence is available. A canary begins with a bounded cohort or traffic share and compares predefined guardrails—error rate, latency, data correctness, and support signals—with a baseline. Choose a minimum observation window that covers relevant behavior, not just a few seconds of quiet traffic. Feature flags can separate deployment from activation, but they add configuration states and must have an owner, secure access, tested defaults, and an expiry or cleanup plan. A rollback may restore old code while leaving an incompatible schema or irreversible external action behind. Pair releases with expand-contract migrations, idempotent operations, and a recovery decision for each stateful change. Define who can halt rollout, how routing is restored, what happens to in-flight work, and how customer impact is communicated. Record evidence and limitations; a canary reduces risk but cannot prove that unobserved workloads are safe.

topics.description: Integrate requirements, boundaries, data, resilience, security, operations, and delivery into a reviewable architecture.

lesson.title: Synthesize a system design with trade-offs and evidence
objectives: Produce a system context and container-level design from explicit requirements.
Justify consistency, failure, security, and recovery decisions.
Present validation evidence, unresolved risks, and evolution triggers.

blocks.title: System-design principle
blocks.body: A system design is a decision set that connects user needs to deployable and operable behavior. Start with functional flows, workload estimates, data sensitivity, and quality attributes; make constraints and uncertainty visible. Draw system context and component boundaries, identify the owner of each datastore, and describe contracts and trust boundaries. Trace one critical write end to end, including idempotency, transaction scope, asynchronous work, duplicate delivery, and reconciliation. Trace one failure from detection through degradation, incident response, backup restore, and customer communication. State an SLI/SLO and capacity budget, then explain how a canary or staged migration limits release risk. Compare at least one alternative and document why its cost is not justified now, along with evidence that would trigger reconsideration. A credible architecture includes operational ownership, runbooks, security tests, and recovery practice. Mark what has only been simulated; diagrams and design documents are plans, not proof of a deployed system's reliability.

practical_project.title: Jirani Harvest: Resilient Order and Dispatch Platform
practical_project.purpose: Design and implement a small, testable simulation of an order workflow for a fictional Kenyan produce cooperative, then produce the system-design and operations artefacts needed to assess how it could evolve. The exercise connects capacity, ownership, consistency, security, reliability, recovery, observability, and controlled change.
privacy_and_limits: Use invented cooperative, order, and location data only; do not enter real farmer, customer, contact, payment, or school records.
Do not connect to a real mobile-money provider, bank, logistics company, cloud account, or production database; simulate external outcomes locally.
A local simulation and design review do not prove production availability, security, disaster recovery, or capacity. Mark every untested operational claim explicitly.
requirements: State functional requirements, peak-workload assumptions, p95 latency goal, availability objective, and capacity headroom with calculation evidence.
Draw system-context and component-boundary diagrams; name the owner of order, stock, and dispatch data and define stable contracts.
Implement or simulate an idempotent order-reservation workflow with transaction boundaries, an outbox or equivalent event record, duplicate handling, and reconciliation.
Specify data indexes, a bounded queue/backpressure rule, cache freshness policy, and a compatible expand-migrate-contract schema change.
Create a threat model with trust boundaries, least-privilege roles, secret-handling rules, mitigations, and residual risks.
Define SLIs/SLOs, error-budget policy, dashboards or synthetic measurements, alert conditions, and an incident runbook.
Write RPO/RTO goals and a simulated restore procedure, canary rollout plan, stop conditions, and rollback or forward-recovery decision.
Provide deterministic tests, a reproducible local setup, architecture decision records, and a final review that distinguishes simulated evidence from production verification.
suggested_steps: Define actors, critical journeys, workload assumptions, data classes, quality attributes, and explicit unknowns.
Draw context and component diagrams; define ownership, API contracts, trust zones, and a critical-write sequence.
Implement the local domain workflow and tests for idempotency, duplicate events, partial failures, and invariants.
Add capacity, queue, caching, migration, threat-model, SLI/SLO, and incident-response artefacts with measurable checks.
Run a controlled local simulation of overload, dependency timeout, and recovery; record what the simulation cannot establish.
Review canary, restore, and evolution plans; present alternatives, trade-offs, residual risks, and evidence-based next steps.
success_checks: Every design choice traces to a user or operational requirement, and alternatives and revisit triggers are documented.
The critical write is repeat-safe in local tests and its consistency/reconciliation limits are explicit.
Capacity, queue, cache, security, SLO, incident, recovery, and rollout decisions have measurable or inspectable evidence.
The restore and incident procedures can be followed as exercises without touching production systems or real personal data.
The report clearly separates implemented code, local simulation, proposed architecture, and unverified production claims.

rubric.look_for: Measurable quality attributes, capacity assumptions, coherent boundaries, ownership, contracts, and trade-off reasoning.
Repeat-safe workflow, transaction/outbox reasoning, bounded work, compatibility migration, and failure containment.
Assets, trust boundaries, least privilege, safe secrets, tests, mitigations, and explicit residual risks.
Useful SLIs/SLOs, actionable signals, incident roles, safe mitigation, communication, and owned learning actions.
Credible RPO/RTO, protected backup and restore exercise, canary guardrails, and data-aware recovery decision.
Deterministic tests, reproducibility, architecture records, limitations, and no unsupported production claims.
